items.title: Steve Turré interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 29, 2021
items.q: Curtis Fuller was Coltrane’s trombone player. That’s saying something.

ctx.x: That’s terrific. Can you recall the first time that you became aware of what improvisation was and the possibilities that you might be able to do it?

I just took a knack to it right away. I didn’t think about all that. I just did it. And in middle school I was playing in a pit band for a ball game, and it was like a little combo. We kind of played New Orleans style. We played “The Saints Go Marching In,” and that kind of, “Muskrat Ramble,” “Bourbon Street Parade,” “Tin Roof Blues,” those were some of the songs we played. So I actually started improvising in the tailgate style, the New Orleans style, before — then in high school somebody gave me a J.J. Johnson…
It is, and as a matter of fact on the way to school this morning I heard a Coltrane recording of “Lazy Bird” and I was speculating that that was Curtis Fuller. I suspect it was.

items.title: Curtis Fuller — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Steve Turre has picked that up. Every time you see him, it’s just “Bam!”

ctx.x: Talk about the music. What is it in the music, then talk about your relationship with ‘Trane, and maybe the date?

‘Trane was my male Billie Holliday. He was like a guru to me. He was like my breathing. Only now, in my old frail age, I get it. I really get it. I understand every phrase, and I try to do that now in my solos just to touch on what ‘Trane was all about. He was a student of Stravinsky, I mean, not going literally to study with the man. But, [he played] sheets of sound. It was almost like bubbling waters sometimes. (Imitates Coltrane’s melody) I didn’t know. I finally got to the place, with the trombone, because…

“No ma’am.” “So, you have the male voice, a baritone voice, the tenor voice. That’s where you are.” Dizzy was saying, “In the middle of that horn, you got it.” I sat next to Al Grey would play a note and you’d hear it five blocks away. But, it’s the context. Key is like the context to the characters of what you play, it’s not how you play it. People that are listening to you, you know? If you say a lot of words, they have to mean something. Check the difference out between, I call them my musical bookends, just…
